## Overview

For asymmetric fp16 W4A16 layers on gfx1151 (Strix Halo), `RDNAHybridW4A16LinearKernel` now trades a little weight memory for faster prefill. At load time, each per-group scale and zero-point is packed into one int32 "carrier". The packed fp16 Triton prefill dequant (#60644) then does one load per (n, group) and a single `v_pk_fma_f16` per pair. Before, it did a scale load, a packed zero-point gather, and a subtract-then-multiply. With the cheaper dequant, asymmetric layers take the packed path from M > 192 (M > 128 when N ≥ 4K) instead of M > 256.

Builds on #60644. Not a duplicate: no open PR adds a scale/zero-point carrier or changes the asymmetric prefill cutoff. #61193 also speeds up gfx1151 prefill, but at M ≥ 4096 by dequantizing to a dense matmul; the two are complementary but touch the same file.

## Claims

- **Batch-1 prefill up to 18% faster end to end.** Qwen3-8B (asymmetric g128): −18.4% at 224 prompt tokens, −17.3% at 256. Qwen3-1.7B (asymmetric g64): −12.1% at 224, −12.4% at 256. No change at 128 tokens, and within ±1.8% from 320 tokens up.
- **No regression at batch 128 and 256** (outputs 1 and 128): Qwen3-8B is 3–11% faster, Qwen3-1.7B 1–5%.
- **Kernel** (geomean over 12 Qwen3 shapes, g128 and g64): 15–18% faster at M 193–256, 4–5% at M 129–192, 1–3% at M 257–4096. At M = 8192, summed over each model's four layers: 12% faster on Qwen3-8B, 5% on Qwen3-1.7B.
- **Memory cost:** 8/G of the int4 weight bytes (6.25% at g128, 12.5% at g64). Measured KV cache is 0.16–0.20% smaller.
- **Accuracy:** GSM8K within one question on both models. Symmetric output is bit-identical to main.
- **Unchanged:** symmetric layers, bf16, g32 (bit-identical to main), the skinny HIP decode path, and every GPU other than gfx1151.

## Validation

gfx1151 (Radeon 8060S, 20 CUs), torch 2.13.0+rocm10.2.0a20260923, Triton 3.8.0. End-to-end runs compare main at `4b47db922b` with this PR rebased on it. Kernel runs compare against main at `0fddee1f58`; `rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py` is identical on both. Each comparison runs both arms on one build, interleaved, alternating which arm goes first per rep.

### End to end: batch-1 prefill latency

This command for each prompt length, 8 runs per arm on main and on this PR. Cells are the median over runs; `~` marks overlapping run ranges.

```
vllm bench latency --model RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16 --dtype float16 \
    --max-model-len 4096 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 256 \
    --no-enable-prefix-caching --seed 0 \
    --batch-size 1 --input-len 224 --output-len 1 \
    --num-iters-warmup 3 --num-iters 15
```

| prompt tokens | Qwen3-8B main → PR (ms) | change | Qwen3-1.7B main → PR (ms) | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 93.7 → 93.6 | −0.1% ~ | 26.3 → 25.2 | −4.2% ~ |
| 160 | 141.4 → 131.3 | **−7.2%** | 36.3 → 34.2 | −5.6% ~ |
| 192 | 142.5 → 134.4 | **−5.7%** | 36.8 → 34.4 | −6.5% ~ |
| 224 | 166.4 → 135.9 | **−18.4%** | 41.5 → 36.4 | **−12.1%** |
| 256 | 168.0 → 138.9 | **−17.3%** | 42.3 → 37.0 | **−12.4%** |
| 320 | 195.4 → 193.1 | −1.2% ~ | 53.8 → 53.4 | −0.8% ~ |
| 384 | 200.9 → 197.4 | −1.8% ~ | 55.0 → 55.4 | +0.8% ~ |
| 512 | 271.6 → 268.9 | −1.0% ~ | 67.7 → 67.0 | −1.0% ~ |
| 1024 | 535.3 → 535.0 | −0.0% ~ | 134.5 → 133.1 | −1.1% ~ |
| 2048 | 1132.9 → 1117.9 | −1.3% | 286.5 → 284.3 | −0.8% ~ |

Control: Qwen3-4B-quantized.w4a16 (symmetric) at 128 / 256 / 512 / 2048 tokens, +0.3% / −0.0% / −0.8% / +0.1%, all overlapping.

### End to end: batch 128 and 256

The same command with `--batch-size 128|256 --input-len 128|512 --output-len 1|128 --num-iters-warmup 1 --num-iters 3`, 3 runs per arm. No cell's run ranges overlap.

| batch | prompt | output | Qwen3-8B main → PR (s) | change | Qwen3-1.7B main → PR (s) | change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 128 | 1 | 9.74 → 8.89 | **−8.8%** | 2.33 → 2.25 | −3.5% |
| 128 | 128 | 128 | 26.28 → 25.51 | −2.9% | 7.16 → 7.07 | −1.2% |
| 128 | 512 | 1 | 39.35 → 35.85 | **−8.9%** | 9.27 → 8.87 | −4.4% |
| 128 | 512 | 128 | 63.04 → 59.98 | −4.9% | 17.35 → 16.98 | −2.1% |
| 256 | 128 | 1 | 19.53 → 17.80 | **−8.8%** | 4.68 → 4.49 | −4.0% |
| 256 | 128 | 128 | 50.22 → 44.83 | **−10.7%** | 13.66 → 12.99 | −4.9% |
| 256 | 512 | 1 | 78.98 → 72.09 | **−8.7%** | 18.51 → 17.88 | −3.4% |
| 256 | 512 | 128 | 123.42 → 113.62 | **−7.9%** | 34.09 → 32.93 | −3.4% |

Prefill at these batch sizes runs in 8192-token chunks, so its GEMMs are at M = 8192. There the PR's kernels take 0.88× main's time on Qwen3-8B and 0.95× on Qwen3-1.7B, summed over each model's four layers. Decode at batch 256 runs at M = 256 and takes the carrier path; decode at batch 128 (M = 128) is unchanged.

### Kernel

`_rdna_hybrid_w4a16_apply_impl` timed with `triton.testing.do_bench`, which flushes cache between reps so weights come from DRAM. 3 reps, median over reps. Shapes: qkv/o/gate_up/down of Qwen3-8B, 4B and 1.7B. Time ratio PR / main, < 1 is faster:

| M | 128 | 129 | 160 | 192 | 193 | 224 | 256 | 257 | 384 | 512 | 1024 | 2048 | 4096 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| g128 geomean | 1.00 | 0.95 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.84 | 0.99 | 0.99 | 0.99 | 0.98 | 0.99 | 0.97 |
| g64 geomean | 1.00 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.96 | 0.83 | 0.84 | 0.85 | 0.99 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| g128 best / worst shape | 1.00 / 1.01 | 0.82 / 1.01 | 0.82 / 1.01 | 0.83 / 1.00 | 0.59 / 1.16 | 0.61 / 1.18 | 0.63 / 1.23 | 0.95 / 1.01 | 0.95 / 1.03 | 0.92 / 1.03 | 0.92 / 1.04 | 0.97 / 1.02 | 0.95 / 0.99 |

The one regression is Qwen3-4B down_proj (N=2560, K=9728) at M 193–256: 1.16–1.24× at g128 and g64. Summed over Qwen3-4B's four layers, asymmetric is still 0.85–0.89× main at g128 (0.87–0.91× at g64) at those M. I did not run asymmetric Qwen3-4B end to end.

At M = 8192, the chunk size at large batch, per layer (g128 Qwen3-8B / g64 Qwen3-1.7B, 3 reps): qkv 0.91 / 0.96, o 0.90 / 0.99, gate_up 0.91 / 0.95, down 0.81 / 0.91.

g32 (no carrier) vs main: bit-identical output in 252/252 cells, time ratio 0.99–1.00 geomean at every M.

### Accuracy

- GSM8K 5-shot, 500 questions, fp16, `tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py` against `vllm serve`, #60644 head → this change: Qwen3-8B 0.884 → 0.882, Qwen3-1.7B 0.654 → 0.652. Each is one question.
- Relative error vs an fp32 dequantize-then-matmul reference: 3.98e-4 with the carrier vs 2.86e-4 without, because `bias_eff` is rounded to fp16.
- Symmetric output is bit-identical to main (168/168 cells).

### Tests

```
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py \
       tests/kernels/quantization/test_w4a16_kernel_selection.py
338 passed, 8 skipped (bf16 carrier cases) on gfx1151
```

New or updated tests:
- prefill GEMM vs the fp32 oracle in symmetric, zero-point and carrier modes;
- `reload_weights` rebuilds the carrier in its original storage.

CI coverage: the AMD quantization-kernels step runs these files on gfx942. There both carrier tests skip, because the GEMM test needs gfx11/gfx12 and the reload test needs gfx1151, so the carrier path is validated on gfx1151 outside CI (above).

### Reproduce

- Kernel: `python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_rdna_hybrid_w4a16_gemm.py --models RedHatAI/Qwen3-8B-quantized.w4a16 --group-size 128`. Compare the `hybrid-w4a16-zp` and `hybrid-w4a16-scale-zp` providers.

## Details

**Carrier layout.** `[N, K//G]` int32: low 16 bits are the fp16 scale, high 16 bits are fp16 `bias_eff = -zp * scale`. Dequant is `(b_raw - 1024) * scale + bias_eff` on the magic-constant unpack from #60644. The output is not bit-identical to the zero-point path, because `bias_eff` is rounded to fp16 and fused into an FMA (see Accuracy).

**Where it is built.** Only asymmetric layers with fp16 scales, g ≥ 64, on gfx1151, the only place the packed dequant runs. On the scalar dequant (fp16 at small M, all bf16) the carrier measured about 1% slower on average with some cells 10–20% slower, since that path is VALU-issue-bound. It is a `Parameter`, so layerwise `reload_weights` recomputes it and copies it into its original storage. A non-persistent buffer would keep its stale value; the new reload test fails with one.

**Why the cutoffs.** Packed tiles with the carrier vs the scalar ladder (time ratio, < 1 favors the carrier), geomean over shapes. Shapes include synthetic K=4096 with N = 3K, 4K, 5K, since no real shape falls between N/K 2.4 and 6.

| g128 | 64 | 96 | 128 | 129 | 160 | 192 | 193 | 224 | 256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N < 4K (10 shapes) | 1.21 | 1.06 | 1.08 | 1.06 | 1.05 | 1.05 | 0.80 | 0.81 | 0.82 |
| N ≥ 4K (5 shapes) | 1.52 | 1.18 | 1.15 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.85 |

- M ≤ 128: the packed path loses on every shape, so it is unchanged.
- M 129–192: N ≥ 4K wins by 16–18%, including the synthetic N = 4K and 5K shapes.
- M > 192: everything wins. The step at 193 is the scalar ladder's 64-row tiles needing a fourth M-tile.
- From M 129 up, g64 matches g128 within 0.02.
- The `N ≥ 4K` rule is conservative: synthetic N = 3K gains 7% at M 129–192 and Qwen3 qkv shapes (N ≥ 6144, N/K 1.5–2.4) gain 6–11%. Every other shape with N ≤ 4096 loses there except Qwen3-4B o_proj (+2–3%). `N > 4096` would fit these 15 shapes better, but I kept the rule that holds without tuning to them.

**Why not g32.** At g32 the carrier would be 12–15% faster than main at M 193–256. From M 257, where main uses the zero-point gather, it is −3% to +2% against it (worst shape +20%), and it costs 25% of the int4 weight bytes. g32 keeps main's path: packed zero-point gather from M > 256.

**Memory.** Decode (`wvSplitK_int4_g`, #57199) still reads the original scales and zero-points, so the carrier is an extra copy. If decode read the carrier instead, those copies could be dropped; that is left for a follow-up.

**Interactions.**
- #60710's opt-in dense weight cache already covers M ≥ 256 when enabled, so with it on the carrier matters only at M 129–256.
- #52637 (open) also changes `process_weights_after_loading` in this file.
- #61193 (open) also edits the prefill dispatch in `rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py`.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the code, tests, benchmarks and this description. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests and benchmarks above.

nodes.body:
I found two existing tests that aren't a great fit:
- `test_reload_weights` (`tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py`) uses Qwen3-0.6B-W4A16-G128, which is symmetric, so no carrier is built. Its few-token prompts also stay on the HIP decode path, which never reads the carrier.
- `test_direct_reload_keeps_kernel_tensor_addresses` (`tests/quantization/test_keep_param_objects.py`) checks exactly this property, but the module only runs on SM100 and only lists NVIDIA kernels.

If this testcase doesn't work we'd end up with some garbage data being used as the carrier data after the reload which could be hard to track down. I am having trouble finding a compelling use-case for reloading for these quantized weights, but it is allowed by the interface. The test itself takes about 1 second on a gfx1151 so I'd feel more comfortable leaving it in since it is fast.

Searching through for these tests also identified a bug. There is both layerwise and direct reloading. direct wasn't handled properly before so I've made that change and parameterized the test on that.

On the scalar dequant (fp16 at small M, all bf16) the carrier measured about 1% slower on average with some cells 10–20% slower, since that path is VALU-issue-bound. It is a `Parameter`, so layerwise `reload_weights` recomputes it and copies it into its original storage. A non-persistent buffer would keep its stale value; the new reload test fails with one.

**Why the cutoffs.** Packed tiles with the carrier vs the scalar ladder (time ratio, < 1 favors the carrier), geomean over shapes. Shapes include synthetic K=4096 with N = 3K, 4K, 5K, since no real shape falls between N/K 2.4 and 6.

| g128 | 64 | 96 | 128 | 129 | 160 | 192 | 193 | 224 | 256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N < 4K (10 shapes) | 1.21 | 1.06 | 1.08 | 1.06 | 1.05 | 1.05 | 0.80 | 0.81 | 0.82 |
| N ≥ 4K (5 shapes) | 1.52 | 1.18 | 1.15 | 0.82 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.85 |

- M ≤ 128: the packed path loses on every shape, so it is unchanged.
- M 129–192: N ≥ 4K wins by 16–18%, including the synthetic N = 4K and 5K shapes.
- M > 192: everything wins. The step at 193 is the scalar ladder's 64-row tiles needing a fourth M-tile.
- From M 129 up, g64 matches g128 within 0.02.
- The `N ≥ 4K` rule is conservative: synthetic N = 3K gains 7% at M 129–192 and Qwen3 qkv shapes (N ≥ 6144, N/K 1.5–2.4) gain 6–11%. Every other shape with N ≤ 4096 loses there except Qwen3-4B o_proj (+2–3%). `N > 4096` would fit these 15 shapes better, but I kept the rule that holds without tuning to them.

**Why not g32.** At g32 the carrier would be 12–15% faster than main at M 193–256. From M 257, where main uses the zero-point gather, it is −3% to +2% against it (worst shape +20%), and it costs 25% of the int4 weight bytes. g32 keeps main's path: packed zero-point gather from M > 256.

**Memory.** Decode (`wvSplitK_int4_g`, #57199) still reads the original scales and zero-points, so the carrier is an extra copy. If decode read the carrier instead, those copies could be dropped; that is left for a follow-up.

**Interactions.**
- #60710's opt-in dense weight cache already covers M ≥ 256 when enabled, so with it on the carrier matters only at M 129–256.
- #52637 (open) also changes `process_weights_after_loading` in this file.
- #61193 (open) also edits the prefill dispatch in `rdna_hybrid_w4a16.py`.

+def pack_scale_zp_carrier(scales: torch.Tensor, zp: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
+    """Fold fp16 per-group scales and packed zero-points into one int32 each.

inline_comments.body:
I found two existing tests that aren't a great fit:
- `test_reload_weights` (`tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py`) uses Qwen3-0.6B-W4A16-G128, which is symmetric, so no carrier is built. Its few-token prompts also stay on the HIP decode path, which never reads the carrier.
- `test_direct_reload_keeps_kernel_tensor_addresses` (`tests/quantization/test_keep_param_objects.py`) checks exactly this property, but the module only runs on SM100 and only lists NVIDIA kernels.

If this testcase doesn't work we'd end up with some garbage data being used as the carrier data after the reload which could be hard to track down. I am having trouble finding a compelling use-case for reloading for these quantized weights, but it is allowed by the interface. The test itself takes about 1 second on a gfx1151 so I'd feel more comfortable leaving it in since it is fast.

Searching through for these tests also identified a bug. There is both layerwise and direct reloading. direct wasn't handled properly before so I've made that change and parameterized the test on that.
